query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The unusual, seemingly disconnected high‐temperature stress–strain and thermoelastic responses of HfNbTaTiZr arise because the alloy’s microstructural evolution (i.e., cold‐work–induced high dislocation density and precipitation‐driven hardening during aging) is synergistically coupled with residual thermal stresses generated by thermal expansion mismatch during cooling/solidification. This interplay creates a dynamic state in which local internal stresses modify the elastic moduli and yield behavior, and control creep rates at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy with relatively uniform dendritic microstructure
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled thermal–mechanical processing comparison by preparing two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: (1) free-standing samples (baseline) and (2) samples processed as part of a composite with a backing material having a significantly lower thermal expansion coefficient to intentionally introduce additional thermal mismatch stresses during cooling.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing over a broad temperature range—from room temperature (≈293 K) up to high temperatures (≈1250 °C) and during aging treatments at 600–800 °C—ensuring that both cold rolling and subsequent thermal exposures are identical aside from the imposed thermal expansion mismatch.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and arrangement of dislocations and the formation of nano-scale precipitates (or local phase transformation products) at grain boundaries, which interact with residual thermal stresses induced by mismatched contraction/expansion during cooling.
generation.mechanism: Cold rolling increases dislocation density and promotes lattice defects that serve as nucleation sites for fine precipitates during aging. When these features are combined with thermal expansion mismatch effects (either intrinsic or imposed in a composite), additional residual stresses are generated at microstructural interfaces. These internal stresses boost local yield strength, alter the elastic response, and modify high-temperature creep behavior by either hindering or channeling dislocation motion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to free-standing samples, the composite samples (with an imposed thermal expansion mismatch) will show higher residual internal stresses, leading to increased yield strength, altered (likely higher) elastic moduli, sharper work hardening after aging, and modified creep rates at high temperatures. These differences should manifest as a shift in the stress–strain response and a change in the temperature dependence of the elastic moduli.
generation.baseline: The free-standing HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibits the previously observed tensile creep behavior at 1250 °C, cold-rolling–induced microhardness changes, elastic moduli varying from 293 to 1100 K, and moderate hardening after aging at 600–800 °C.
generation.boundary: The predicted effects are expected primarily within the temperature range where both dislocation-mediated processes and thermal expansion mismatches are active (i.e., from room temperature up to about 1250 °C), and in the microstructural regime where the precipitate volume fraction and dislocation density have not reached saturation; if precipitation coarsening dominates or if the imposed expansion mismatch is below a critical threshold, the contribution may be minimal.
generation.uncertainty: The relative quantitative contributions of microstructural hardening versus residual thermal stresses remain uncertain, as does the critical threshold of thermal expansion mismatch required to induce measurable changes. In addition, the possible interaction with oxidation effects at the highest temperatures may add complexity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr alloy specimens under identical thermal and mechanical histories aside from the embedding condition: one set as free-standing bars and another set as composites laminated onto a substrate with a lower thermal expansion coefficient. Subject both sets to identical aging treatments (600–800 °C), cold rolling, and high-temperature tensile/creep tests spanning from RT up to 1250 °C.
measurements: Elastic modulus (via dynamic mechanical analysis or resonant ultrasound spectroscopy)
Steady-state creep rate at high temperatures
Residual stress levels (e.g., using X-ray/neutron diffraction)
Microstructural characterization (dislocation density, precipitate size and distribution via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composite samples do not display statistically significant differences in yield strength, elastic modulus, work hardening behavior, or high-temperature creep rate relative to the free-standing baseline samples, then the hypothesis that the coupling of microstructural evolution with thermal expansion–induced residual stresses governs the alloy’s unconventional behavior would be falsified.

After discussing the law of strength change with temperature and analyzing the results of the transmission electron microscopy, it is concluded that the deformation of the alloy at high temperature is mainly controlled by dislocation, and the morphology and density of the dislocation control the mechanical properties of the alloy. We have not discussed the plasticity change before, so the next focus is to analyze the change in alloy plasticity at high temperature and the reasons for that change. In high-temperature tensile tests, the strength of the alloy is more important, but the plasticity changes are equally important. In this study, it was obtained that the fracture plasticity of the alloy diminishes as the temperature rises (except at 673 K) (See Figure 4b). cited_evidence.text: The formation of solidification cracks is the combined result of the intergranular low-melting-point liquid film and large tensile stress acting on the weld. Fig. 6 illustrates the experimental thermal expansion coefficient of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA. According to the figure, the thermal expansion coefficient of the alloy at 900–1100 K varies between 23 × 10−6 and 25 × 10−6, which is higher than that of austenitic stainless steel (16 × 10−6–17 × 10−6 K−1) in the same temperature range. Hence, the welded joints of the alloy will result in greater tensile stresses during solidification, and they are more susceptible to thermal cracking. Meanwhile, compared to the stainless steel plate, the aluminum alloy base plate has higher thermal conductivity. This indicates that the heat dissipation is more rapid and the weld cooling rate is faster, leading to a larger tensile strain rate. In other words, in the late stages of weld solidification, the proportion of solid phase increases, so the residual liquid metal spreads over the grain boundaries of dendrites to form a thin liquid film.
